html:
A user story is not a spec you hand to a developer — it is a promise of a future conversation. This phase teaches you to write INVEST-compliant stories, translate BrightLogistics' epics into shippable slices, and run a backlog the team can rank by numbers instead of feelings. Your lab is the User_Story__c object and the BacklogPrioritizationService class in force-app, and the skill sits at the center of the CBA blueprint (User Story Creation is 18% of the exam).

Learning Objectives

  • Write user stories in the "As a... I want... so that..." format to open a requirements conversation...
  • Apply all six INVEST criteria and identify which letter a vague story breaks...
  • Define measurable acceptance criteria using Given/When/Then scenarios a tester can verify...
  • Break epics into small, independently deployable, value-shipping stories...
  • Build a story map that sequences user jobs against releases...
  • Prioritize a backlog with a weighted Value/Effort/Risk model and defend the ranking to stakeholders...
  • Operate the User_Story__c object fields and the BacklogPrioritizationService account in the repo...
  • Run a backlog refinement session that produces resized, re-ranked, clarified stories...

1. The Story Formula and Format

Every user story is three sentences wearing the same costume: a role, a desired capability, and the benefit the capability produces.

md
As a <role>
I want <capability>
so that <benefit>

The first line names the actor — a sales rep, a dispatcher, a reviewer. The second names the behavior in the system; the third is the value that survives a canceled feature. In BrightLogistics, a story might read:

md
As a dispatcher
I want overdue leads to appear highlighted on my work queue
so that I can route the highest-risk inbound leads first.

Notice what the story does not say: no field names, no buttons. The role anchors every later debate in the user's context — the BA is the team's memory of WHY (Phase 7). Write the benefit in the user's language: "so that I can route leads faster" beats "so that the Lead object is updated". The story is deliberately informal — the starting point of a conversation, never the full contract; the contract lives in the acceptance criteria (section 5).

2. INVEST: Independent and Negotiable

INVEST — Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable — is the checklist you read each story against before it enters a sprint.

Independent means the team can build and deliver a story in any order. If story B works only after A, you have written one story cut in half. "Route web leads to the right tier" and "Notify the assignee" are independent even though one usually precedes the other. Dependency becomes preference of ordering, not necessity; when a story "depends on" the one before it, re-slice.

Negotiable means the story is a promise of a conversation, not a frozen contract. A story that over-specifies the implementation — "Add a picklist field to the Lead page layout" — is a work order, not a story. Negotiable stories state the outcome and leave the team latitude on the how; the acceptance criteria form the boundary.

3. INVEST: Valuable, Estimable, Small

Valuable means the story ships benefit to one real user by itself, stated in the "so that" clause in a way the user would notice. Slice to a single user role so value is not split across audiences — "Add activity history to the lead record" names the rep who stops switching tools.

Estimable means the team can size it — guesses compound across a sprint. A story is usually un-estimable because it is vague ("various improvements") or hides unknowns (an unseen integration). The fix is decomposition or a spike story whose only deliverable is an answer.

Small means the story is completable within the sprint — two days or less of effort in this academy, about one story point a day. Bigger stories resist mid-sprint inspection and make "done" mean "mostly done". Slice by user, workflow step, or data type until each slice ships alone. The repo enforces Small: the validation rule on Story_Points__c in force-app/main/default/objects/User_Story__c/ caps a story at 21 points.

4. INVEST: Testable

Testable is the final and most exacting letter. A story is testable when a tester can look at the system and say pass or fail without debating interpretation. "Various performance improvements" fails; "the lead page renders in under 2 seconds at 1,000 leads with no more than 200ms beyond baseline" passes. An acceptance criterion that cannot be checked by a tester is not done — write it so a tester can verify it.

Self-check: a story says "so that the process is more efficient." Which INVEST letter breaks? Testable (and Estimable) — "efficient" is vague; add a measurable criterion like "cycle time under 4 hours" before the story enters a sprint.

For a Salesforce BA, testability translates into data states — "Given a lead with 3 logged activities, When I open the lead page, Then I see the activities sorted newest first" is a scenario UAT can literally execute, the bridge to Phase 12 where each criterion becomes a UAT_Test_Case__c record.

5. Acceptance Criteria and Given/When/Then

Acceptance criteria turn the story's promise into a verdict. The most reliable format is Given/When/Then, borrowed from behavior-driven development because it is symmetric with how testers verify and how dashboards measure:

gherkin
Given <initial data state>
When <the user performs an action>
Then <the observable, verifiable outcome>

Write multiple scenarios where the story deserves them — happy path, empty state, boundary state, error path. For the workhorse example in this repo's lead activity story:

gherkin
Given a lead with 3 logged activities
When I open the lead page
Then I see the activities sorted newest first.

Given a lead with 0 logged activities
When I open the lead page
Then I see an empty state panel with a "Log activity" action.

Three habits keep criteria crisp:

  • Use concrete numbers, dates, and status values — "sorted newest first" becomes "sorted by Activity Date descending".
  • One rule per scenario; combine scenarios, never rules, into a paragraph.

Every criterion you accept here becomes a test case in UAT (Phase 12) and a wireframe element in Phase 8. If a criterion has no home on the wireframe, it silently drifts away during delivery — renegotiate it before it slips.

6. Breaking Epics into Stories

An epic is a big, vaguely-shaped body of work spanning releases. The BA's skill is carving it without losing the value logic:

EpicSliced stories
Lead assignment overhaulRoute web leads to the right tier · Notify the assignee · Reassign when queues are busy
UAT readinessCapture test cases · Log defects · Gate sign-off per story
Adoption dashboardPipeline conversion · License usage · Training completion

Slice along three axes:

  • By user — the dispatcher's routing story vs. the executive's dashboard story are different slices of the same dashboards.
  • By workflow step — capture, then log, then sign off; each step is independently valuable and demoable.
  • By data type — report on leads first, opportunities later, if value and risk differ.

Each slice must ship value alone — that independence is why the team can demo frequently and why the backlog can be re-ranked by value rather than forced into a dependency chain. A story over two days of work is usually not sliced enough: reduce scope, split audiences, or defer a boundary case to a follow-up story, and note the boundary so it does not silently vanish.

7. Story Mapping

Story mapping arranges stories on a grid with the user's journey steps running left to right and release slices running top to bottom. The left-to-right axis is the backbone of the user's job as they actually do it. For BrightLogistics the backbone reads: capture lead, qualify, assign, dispatch, follow up. Under each step the team stacks the supporting stories, most essential first, and the top row becomes Release 1: a complete walkable journey, with Release 2 next.

The map democratizes prioritization: a stakeholder sees a missing step as a physical gap, moving arguments from "I want this story higher" to "my step has no backbone column". It enforces Valuable and Small because gaps and oversized stones surface visibly.

8. Backlog Prioritization with Weighted Scoring

When a backlog has more stories than sprints, the team must order them — and scoring beats shouting. The repo's weighted model in force-app/main/default/classes/BacklogPrioritizationService.cls computes a priority index from Value, Effort, and Risk:

apex
// BacklogPrioritizationService.scoreStories()
// index = value weight - effort/risk penalty -> higher first
@InvocableMethod(label='Score stories' description='Recompute backlog priority')
public static void scoreStories(List<Id> storyIds) {
  for (User_Story__c s : [SELECT Id, Priority__c, Story_Points__c
                          FROM User_Story__c WHERE Id IN :storyIds]) {
    Integer valueWeight = s.Priority__c == 'Must Have' ? 5
                        : s.Priority__c == 'Should Have' ? 4
                        : s.Priority__c == 'Could Have' ? 3 : 1;
    Integer effort = Integer.valueOf(s.Story_Points__c == null ? 1 : s.Story_Points__c);
    s.Priority_Score__c = valueWeight * 10 - effort;   // see SERVICE for the full model
  }
}

The class embeds the classic MoSCoW weight (Must Have, Should Have, Could Have) pulled from each story's Priority__c value, subtracts an effort penalty from Story_Points__c, and writes the result to Priority_Score__c. The full production model also folds in a risk penalty and urgency multiplier — read the class comments for the complete formula.

Two numbers drive the ranking: value (and urgency) against effort and risk; high value, low effort wins. Because the model is a number on a record, debates become "why does the score say X when we felt Y?" — arguments about weights, not feelings. Re-rank at every refinement: priorities decay as the business changes.

9. The User_Story__c Object in the Repository

All of this comes together in the User_Story__c object (metadata under force-app/main/default/objects/User_Story__c/), whose fields make backlog management measurable:

FieldPurpose in the workflow
NameThe story title — the capability, tersely
Priority__cMoSCoW weight used by the scoring model
Story_Points__cEffort estimate, capped by validation rule at 21
Priority_Score__cThe computed index written by BacklogPrioritizationService
Status__cLifecycle state driven by the User_Story_Status_Transition flow

Status__c is not a free-form text box; it is a governed lifecycle. The User_Story_Status_Transition flow in force-app/main/default/flows/User_Story_Status_Transition.flow-meta.xml moves stories from Backlog through Refined, In Progress, Done (and back), so a story cannot skip refinement or be marked Done without passing a gate. Pair the flow with UserStoryService (force-app/main/default/classes/UserStoryService.cls), which validates INVEST concerns and acceptance criteria when a story changes — the declarative route and the Apex route to the same business rule, exactly the Phase 9 lesson writ small.

10. Backlog Refinement

Backlog refinement is the regular meeting where stories get ready, not done. The team answers three questions for the next batch: Is it understood? Is it small? Is it still worth the rank it holds? Outputs are resized stories, clarified acceptance criteria, updated scores, and a clear "ready" list.

The BA's preparation for refinement mirrors the artifacts you now know:

  • Re-run the scoring model — any story whose business context changed gets re-ranked.
  • Read each story against INVEST — flag the letters that break and bring re-slice options.
  • Re-read the acceptance criteria with a tester's eyes — anything unverifiable returns to the author.
  • Confirm the story map gaps — a step with no stories is a conversation to have.

Run refinement on the next 5-10 stories, not the whole backlog — a 40-minute standup is the symptom of unrefined stories (Phase 7). The BA records decisions, owners, and follow-ups, and the changes land on the User_Story__c records the same evening.

11. Common Pitfalls and the BA Checklist

Years of story-writing produce the same failures:

  • The "various" story — vague language breaks Testable and Estimable. Add numbers, dates, and statuses.
  • The dependency chain — stories that can only build in one order violate Independent. Re-slice.
  • The epic in a story's body — if the acceptance criteria describe three workflows, it is an epic wearing a story costume.
  • Correctness without value — passing every criterion with no stated benefit is useless.
  • Scoring once — priorities decay; re-rank at every refinement.
  • Unverifiable criteria — if a tester cannot say pass/fail, the story is not done being written.

Before a story enters a sprint, run the checklist: role named, benefit stated, INVEST passes, criteria are Given/When/Then and verifiable, score computed, status transition legal.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 6.1 — Write INVEST-Compliant Stories for BrightLogistics

Steps:

  1. Take the epic "Lead assignment overhaul" from this guide's section 6 and slice it into at least three stories.
  2. For each slice, write the "As a / I want / so that" formula and label the user role.
  3. Score each letter of INVEST against your draft and fix any that break.

Expected result: three stories, each with a one-line role, a one-line capability, a one-line benefit, all six INVEST letters passing. What it proves: slicing an epic is a design decision, not a typing exercise.

Exercise 6.2 — Convert Acceptance Criteria to Given/When/Then

Steps:

  1. Take the story "Notify the assignee when a qualified lead is routed" and draft conventional bullet criteria.
  2. Rewrite them as Given/When/Then scenarios, including an empty state and an error path.
  3. Trade with a partner and check each other's scenarios for verifiability.

Expected result: at least three scenarios a tester could execute against the org without asking questions. What it proves: the format forces testable, concrete criteria.

Exercise 6.3 — Operate the Scoring Model in the Lab

Steps:

  1. Open Setup in the lab org and add four User_Story__c records with mixed Priority__c (Must Have..Won't Have) and Story_Points__c (1, 5, 13, 21).
  2. Run BacklogPrioritizationService (via the Backlog_Prioritization_Scoring flow or an anonymous Apex call) and inspect Priority_Score__c on each record.
  3. Re-sort the list view by Priority_Score__c descending and sanity-check the order by hand against the formula.

Expected result: the records sort in the order the formula predicts; find the one where a 21-point story sinks below a smaller Must Have. What it proves: scoring makes prioritization a debate about weights, not feelings. (This is the spirit of exercise 6.3 in Phase 15.)

Exercise 6.4 — Run a 20-Minute Refinement

Steps:

  1. Pull your four story records and the story map from section 7 into a spreadsheet.
  2. Lead a 20-minute refinement with your study group: decide "ready" or "not ready" per story, re-rank one whose context changed, slice one that is oversized.
  3. Record decisions and owners, then update the records in the org.

Expected result: a "ready" list of stories with updated scores and owners, plus a handful of re-slice notes. What it proves: refinement is the ceremony where INVEST, mapping, and scoring converge. (Revisit the broader 6.4 backlog drills in Phase 15.)

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
User storyA promise of a conversation: "As a <role> I want <capability> so that <benefit>".
INVESTSix criteria for a healthy story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
Acceptance criteriaThe conditions a tester uses to decide the story is done.
Given/When/ThenA scenario format pairing a data state, a user action, and a verifiable outcome.
EpicA large body of work sliced into stories across releases.
Story mappingA grid of journey steps by release slices exposing gaps and dependencies.
MoSCoWMust Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have — priority classes used as scoring weights.
BacklogThe ordered list of user stories awaiting scheduling into sprints.
Backlog refinementThe ceremony that re-slices, re-sizes, re-scores, and clarifies upcoming stories.
Priority_Score__cThe priority index computed by BacklogPrioritizationService.

Certification Checkpoints

  • Write a user story in the standard three-line format with a distinct role and benefit...
  • Identify which INVEST letter a given story violates and explain the fix...
  • Convert acceptance criteria into verifiable Given/When/Then scenarios...
  • Slice an enterprise epic into independently deployable stories...
  • Justify a backlog ranking using the repo's weighted Value/Effort model...
  • Explain the role of User_Story__c fields and the story status lifecycle in Phase 9's flow...
  • Outline the inputs and outputs of a backlog refinement session...

Summary

You can now write the promise — the three-line user story — and keep it honest with INVEST, measurable with Given/When/Then criteria, shippable with epics sliced small, and ranked by numbers instead of emotions through BacklogPrioritizationService. You can operate the User_Story__c lab records and run a refinement that produces a ready list, not more debate. That is the User Story Creation area of the CBA blueprint — and the foundation every Agile ceremony in Phase 7 stands on.
